locations.anchorExact: From the thesis perspective, this chapter occupies a distinct position. It keeps the note-level MIDI velocity target and the score-informed VeloEst architecture introduced in Chapter~\ref{ch:scoreinf}, but it relaxes the assumption that ground-truth velocity labels are available for the target instrument. It complements Chapter~\ref{ch:audiodyn}, which addressed Scenario~S3 with a different output (beat-synchronous score dynamics), by extending the velocity-focused work to a label-scarce setting. The chapter therefore contributes to thesis Requirement~R5 by combining numerical diagnostics, perceptual loudness correlations, and renderer-robust evaluation evidence, and to Requirement~R6 by treating beyond-piano transfer as a missing-supervision problem rather than ordinary acoustic domain shift.

locations.anchorExact: MIDI velocity is a different kind of representation. It is attached to a note onset rather than to a phrase or region. In conventional MIDI performance data, a sounding note onset carries a discrete velocity value on a finite integer scale. In a chord, each note may have a different velocity. In a rapid passage, every note can carry its own local attack value. MIDI velocity is therefore a micro-level representation: it serialises note-level actions rather than summarising the expressive state of a passage.
locations.proposedEnglish: The target studied here is MIDI Note On velocity: a discrete control value attached to the start of a note. This definition is narrower than the full MIDI protocol, which also includes Note Off velocity, aftertouch, and continuous controllers. The thesis estimates one onset value per note rather than a time-varying control trajectory.

locations.anchorExact:
The word \emph{velocity} is often described informally as key-strike force. For keyboard instruments this is useful but imprecise. In sensor-equipped acoustic pianos, the recorded value is more accurately treated as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion near the note attack. Studies of computer-controlled pianos distinguish the player's physical action, the hammer--string interaction, the measured control value, and the resulting acoustic signal \cite{goebl2003role,goebl2004piano}. Large piano datasets such as MAESTRO use this property to provide aligned audio and MIDI data with key-strike velocity labels, making note-level velocity a practical target for MIR systems \cite{hawthorne2019maestro}.

MIDI velocity is exact as symbolic data. A note with velocity 80 remains velocity 80 when the MIDI file is copied, edited, or passed to a model. It is also mechanical in the sense that it refers to a local performance control: how strongly a note attack is executed or how strongly a synthesiser should respond. This objectivity is one reason why velocity is attractive for automatic transcription, expressive rendering, and symbolic performance modelling \cite{ewert2011est,kim2023score,kim2024method}.

However, exactness in the data structure does not imply universality in sound. MIDI velocity is not loudness, not amplitude, and not a dynamic marking. It is a control parameter whose acoustic effect depends on the instrument, renderer, register, sample layer, synthesis design, and recording chain. Dannenberg's analysis of MIDI velocity shows that different synthesisers and patches implement substantially different velocity-response curves \cite{dan2006psy}. Thus, a MIDI value can be objective without being perceptually absolute. It is exact as a note-level control value, but relative as an acoustic and musical quantity.

locations.anchorExact: Originating from the physical sensors of electronic keyboards and pianos, MIDI velocity is a machine-centric measurement of physical intensity. To say it operates as a "note-level" parameter means that every music note from a discrete key strike is assigned an independent, static integer representing its initial strike force. This strict per-note measurement dictates that velocity functions as a discrete loudness control parameter. It is highly granular and absolute within its own scale, yet the resulting loudness highly depends on the acoustic environment and the specific instrument being played. Because MIDI velocity is necessary for MIDI-to-audio playback in DAWs and synthesisers, a common default is set to 64 when it is missing.
locations.proposedEnglish: Here, MIDI velocity refers to the velocity value in a Note On message. It is a machine-readable control parameter. In sensor-equipped piano data, the recorded value acts as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion. Each note carries an integer value that can be edited independently, although its acoustic effect depends on the instrument and renderer. When expressive values are missing, a MIDI sequence may instead use a constant such as 64.

locations.anchorExact: Dynamic markings are the conventional score vocabulary for notated loudness and dynamic change. They include static markings such as \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mp}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}, as well as directional indications such as \textit{crescendo}, \textit{diminuendo}, and hairpins. Although a marking is printed at a specific visual position, its musical scope is usually broader than that position. A single \textit{p} may govern a phrase, a texture, or a formal region until a later marking or musical event changes the dynamic state. A crescendo indicates a tendency over a span, not an isolated value at one note.

alternative_locations_evidence.anchorExact: From a machine-learning perspective, score-dynamics recovery can be framed as classification or structured sequence labelling. The input is audio. The output is a sequence of dynamic symbols or dynamic regimes. The choice of audio representation is therefore not neutral. In the MazurkaBL line of work, the performed-loudness side of this mapping is extracted through sone-based psychoacoustic processing rather than raw amplitude, precisely because the target concerns perceived intensity rather than unweighted energy \cite{kosta2017thesis}. More generally, perceptual front-ends such as Bark-scale specific loudness preserve both a scalar loudness trajectory and the Bark-wise distribution of loudness across the spectrum, which gives a better inductive bias for loudness-oriented tasks than log-Mel features \cite{narang2024automatic,he2026dynest}. Figure~\ref{fig:bg_temporal_units}(a)--(c) shows this contrast on the same excerpt. The practical consequence is also clear: a Nyquist-constrained Bark front-end is substantially lower-dimensional than a $128$-band log-Mel representation, which enables longer audio segments and the phrase-level context that score dynamics actually requires. The challenge is that the labels themselves are sparse, relative, and musically contextual rather than physically absolute. This is one reason why a beat-synchronous formulation is more natural than direct frame-wise regression of continuous loudness.
alternative_locations_evidence.proposedEnglish: Besides static levels, score dynamics includes gradual indications such as crescendo and diminuendo, as described in Section 2.3.1. Chapter 5 estimates the five static levels available in its annotations and their change points; it does not explicitly decode these longer-span symbols.

locations.anchorExact: The empirical claims of this thesis are conditioned on what each available dataset can support. Table~\ref{tab:dataset_comparison} summarises the representative corpora relevant to expressive label recovery, listing their instrument coverage, scale, and which expressive modalities (MIDI velocity, score, and score dynamics) are actually available. The MIDI column also includes note annotations that can be converted to MIDI, such as the JAMS annotations in GuitarSet. The discussion that follows turns these modality differences into chapter-specific constraints.

alternative_locations_evidence.proposedEnglish: Representative datasets relevant to expressive label recovery, separating audio access, note annotations, velocity annotations, reference scores, and score-dynamics annotations. The provenance of velocity annotations is specified in the row notes. A tick indicates the stated modality, a cross indicates its absence, and a triangle refers to a qualification in the corresponding row note. The audio column distinguishes available performance recordings, externally linked recordings, and software-rendered material. For ATEPP, the reported 43% applies to score availability; the dynamic markings in those scores have not been verified.

locations.anchorExact: Score dynamics is usually evaluated as classification on a musically meaningful grid. F1 score is common because the class distribution is imbalanced and because some symbols occur much less frequently than others \cite{kosta2017thesis}. In the present thesis, beat-synchronous evaluation is especially important because it avoids arbitrary frame-level tolerance choices and aligns the prediction target with how the annotations are actually used in music notation.
locations.proposedEnglish: For a given class or event type, precision is TP/(TP+FP), recall is TP/(TP+FN), and F1 is 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN), where TP, FP, and FN are true positives, false positives, and false negatives. Macro-F1 averages the class-wise scores equally, whereas support-weighted F1 weights them by their reference counts. These averages answer different questions and must be identified when reporting score-dynamics results. Note-level velocity MAE averages the absolute prediction error over the reference note onsets; its full definition and the complementary dispersion metrics are given in Section 3.6.3.

locations.anchorExact: Velocity should be evaluated at note level rather than by naive frame-wise error. Otherwise, long sustained notes dominate the metric. Standard statistics include mean absolute error and related dispersion measures \cite{kuo2021velocity,kim2024method}. However, numerical accuracy alone is not sufficient. A model can achieve a decent average error while producing over-smoothed or mechanically centred dynamics. Distribution-sensitive measures, visual inspection, and listening tests therefore play an important complementary role. This is especially evident in Chapter~\ref{ch:velcomp}, where perceptual differences are not always fully captured by raw error.

author_reply_exact:
Good question. The idea originally came from image-processing papers, especially the use of U-Net and window attention. We use “image-based” because both the input and output are two-dimensional pitch–time matrices, processed with two-dimensional convolutions.

The input is a binary piano roll, and the output is a single-channel velocity roll. We do not predict RGB colours. “Colourisation” is an analogy for adding velocity values to the existing note structure, it's good for general audiance understand, but I agree that the wording needs clarification.

I would say the “image-like” is more proper. I will make revision.

locations.anchorExact:
To process MIDI as images, we convert each performance into three matrices of size \(T \times P\), where \(T\) is the number of time frames and \(P=88\) is the number of piano pitches.
The three matrices are a binary onset roll \(O\), marking note starts; a binary frame roll \(F\), indicating note activation over time; and a velocity roll \(V\), acting as the target colour intensity.
In the implemented system, \(F\) is the network input, \(V\) is the prediction target, and \(O\) is used for onset masking in the loss.
For the velocity roll, integer values in \([0,127]\) are normalised to \([0,1)\) to match the model output activation range.
During post-processing, the model output is denormalised by scaling and rounding back to integer MIDI velocity.
As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:velcomp_model}, these matrices are highly sparse.

locations.anchorExact: MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) is the dominant symbolic format in modern music production. A MIDI file that resembles sheet music can still sound mechanical when its note velocities are undefined or flattened to a default constant. In contrast, MIDI captured from human performance preserves the performer's control of intensity and therefore carries a substantial portion of the perceived musical expression. As discussed in the thesis introduction, dynamics is the expressive dimension targeted first in this thesis because it is both perceptually salient and directly editable. This chapter studies the most constrained setting in that map: recovering note-level MIDI velocity when the symbolic notes and their timing are already known.

locations.anchorExact:
\paragraph{Procedure.}
Participants were instructed to use headphones because the relevant velocity differences are subtle and are easier to judge at adequate playback quality and level.
In each trial, the audio rendered from the human-performed MIDI served as the fixed reference, and the rendered system outputs were judged relative to that reference.
Following a MUSHRA-inspired reference-based procedure \cite{series2014mursha}, participants rated each processed stimulus independently on a continuous 0--5 scale, where the labelled intervals corresponded to ``bad'', ``poor'', ``fair'', ``good'', and ``excellent'' similarity.
The final scores were averaged across listeners to obtain MOS, and 95\% confidence intervals were computed for reporting.

locations.anchorExact: Given a piano performance audio signal, the system predicts four synchronised output sequences on a frame grid: dynamic levels, dynamic change points, beats, and downbeats. The dynamic targets are the score-facing outputs, while beats and downbeats provide the metrical structure required to align these labels to a symbolic score. This joint design serves two practical modes of use. In the first mode, a reliable beat grid is already available from an aligned score or a score-level AMT system, and the predicted dynamic labels are attached to that grid. In the second mode, no score is available, and the model first predicts beats and downbeats by itself, then uses the estimated grid to place the dynamic labels.
locations.proposedEnglish: These outputs could be attached to the note content of a score-level AMT system to produce dynamics-annotated notation. The present experiments evaluate dynamics and metrical estimation separately from note transcription, so they do not establish the performance of a complete integrated AMT system or an improvement in note-detection accuracy.

locations.anchorExact: More specifically, the dynamic-level target is formulated as a six-class frame-wise prediction problem, including one \textit{blank} class before the first annotated marking and the five score-dynamics classes used in MazurkaBL: \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}. The change-point target is binary and indicates whether a contextual transition between adjacent dynamic regimes occurs at a given time. Beats and downbeats are also binary frame-wise targets. At inference time, the frame-wise outputs are converted into beat-synchronous score annotations by sampling the dynamic class at beat locations and snapping detected change points to the nearest beat.

locations.anchorExact: The model outputs frame-wise probabilities, which are converted into discrete musical events through tailored post-processing. For beat and downbeat detection, we use the thresholding and local-maximum peak-picking steps of \cite{foscarin2024beat}: probabilities are thresholded at 50\%, and peak picking is applied within a 7-frame local neighbourhood (radius 3 at 50~fps). For dynamic markings, the dynamic level at each beat is determined by taking the \texttt{argmax} of the class probabilities at that frame. When an external beat grid is available, this sampling step is performed on that grid; otherwise, the model's own beat predictions are used, which gives the fully end-to-end mode considered in this chapter.

This protocol is intended as a reproducible transfer diagnostic: it asks whether a MazurkaBL-trained fold checkpoint can be reused on an external classical-piano corpus, while the main MazurkaBL table remains the within-corpus benchmark reported as mean and standard deviation over all folds. The per-fold outputs are retained so that the selected fold can be traced.

locations.anchorExact: The cross-dataset results make this distinction more concrete. If score dynamics were merely a continuous loudness variable relabelled into five fixed bins, an out-of-domain corpus with compatible audio quality would mainly cause smooth calibration errors. Instead, Vienna4x22 shows that the symbolic prior itself matters: a passage that is moderate in acoustic intensity may be notated as \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, or \textit{f} depending on the local phrase, edition, and corpus convention. A model trained on MazurkaBL carries a learned expectation about how often each of these labels should occur, and this expectation can become wrong even when the metrical grid remains reasonably stable. The model is therefore learning an acoustic, metrical, and editorial mapping at the same time.

locations.anchorExact: Two limitations of waveform-level supervision are relevant here. First, a Diff-Synth only approximates the real instrument; its waveform statistics differ from real recordings in timbre, articulation, microphone response, and room acoustics. A waveform or spectral loss therefore spends much of its gradient budget on residual mismatch rather than on velocity-dependent behaviour. Second, an instrument-specific Diff-Synth requires a dedicated design: piano-oriented synthesisers expect piano-specific controls such as pedal state, while guitar-oriented synthesisers expect string-wise trajectories. Reusing one Diff-Synth across instruments is therefore impractical.

locations.anchorExact: Velocity is not the only MIDI control that shapes rendered dynamics: continuous controllers can also encode within-note loudness variation~\cite{ryu2024midfild}. Pedal settings and room response also affect the synthesised piano waveform and are explicitly modelled by DDSP-Piano~\cite{renault2023ddsp_piano}. Consequently, when adaptation updates only velocity, the velocity gradient can become entangled with residuals caused by fixed or unobserved controls. Diff-SFProxy avoids this contamination by treating velocity as the only loudness-shaping degree of freedom, but the choice carries its own cost. The recovered velocity absorbs effects that, in the real performance, came from other parallel controls.

locations.anchorExact: Given a piano performance audio signal, the system predicts four synchronised output sequences on a frame grid: dynamic levels, dynamic change points, beats, and downbeats. The dynamic targets are the score-facing outputs, while beats and downbeats provide the metrical structure required to align these labels to a symbolic score. This joint design serves two practical modes of use. In the first mode, a reliable beat grid is already available from an aligned score or a score-level AMT system, and the predicted dynamic labels are attached to that grid. In the second mode, no score is available, and the model first predicts beats and downbeats by itself, then uses the estimated grid to place the dynamic labels.

The technical chapters do address this question through speciﬁc recovery scenarios, such as symbolic velocity completion, score-informed velocity correction, audio-only score-dynamics recovery, and beyond-piano proxy-supervised velocity estimation. I recommend a minor revision in which each technical chapter includes a short opening or closing paragraph that explains how that chapter addresses the central question under its speciﬁc data-availability condition. locations.anchorExact: Originating from the physical sensors of electronic keyboards and pianos, MIDI velocity is a machine-centric measurement of physical intensity. To say it operates as a "note-level" parameter means that every music note from a discrete key strike is assigned an independent, static integer representing its initial strike force. This strict per-note measurement dictates that velocity functions as a discrete loudness control parameter. It is highly granular and absolute within its own scale, yet the resulting loudness highly depends on the acoustic environment and the specific instrument being played. Because MIDI velocity is necessary for MIDI-to-audio playback in DAWs and synthesisers, a common default is set to 64 when it is missing.
locations.proposedEnglish: Here, MIDI velocity refers to the velocity value in a Note On message. It is a machine-readable control parameter. In sensor-equipped piano data, the recorded value acts as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion. Each note carries an integer value that can be edited independently, although its acoustic effect depends on the instrument and renderer. When expressive values are missing, a MIDI sequence may instead use a constant such as 64.

sectionPath.section_title: Unified Thesis Question and Three Core Scenarios

T01.proposedEnglish: Here, weakly expressive data retain note content and timing but have simplified dynamics, such as constant or coarsely quantised velocities. Weak supervision refers to learning without reliable direct dynamics labels, using indirect evidence such as the renderer-based supervision in Chapter~\ref{ch:beyondpiano}. These conditions can overlap.
T01.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

sectionPath.section_title: Unified Thesis Question and Three Core Scenarios

T02.proposedEnglish: Chapter~\ref{ch:beyondpiano} extends S2 to guitar when target-domain velocity labels are unavailable. It retains the score-informed estimator and aligned note events. Audio-only velocity adaptation remains future work; S3 instead targets score dynamics.
T02.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T03.anchorExact: This motivates the image-based view adopted in the present chapter. By treating symbolic MIDI as a sparse image and velocity as a colourisation target, the model can exploit local polyphonic structure more directly. U-Net and attention mechanisms are already successful in related music and audio tasks, but the present setting is distinct because it is purely symbolic and does not rely on acoustic input \cite{he2025filling,kim2024method}. This makes the chapter a natural starting point for the broader thesis.
T03.proposedEnglish: We use a piano roll to place simultaneous notes and local pitch--time neighbourhoods on a regular grid for the convolutional U-Net. The input is binary; the single-channel output supplies velocity values, so colourisation is an analogy for adding dynamics to existing notes. A note-list representation would require a different model interface \cite{he2025filling,kim2024method}.
T03.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T04.anchorExact: This separation of roles is important. The acoustic branch still provides the initial evidence for performance intensity. The score does not overwrite that evidence. Instead, it regularises the estimate by telling the model where notes occur and how they are organised in time. Later results will show that this division of labour is strong enough to improve both in-domain accuracy and cross-dataset behaviour.
T04.proposedEnglish: Note detection and velocity estimation may benefit from joint modelling, but this chapter evaluates velocity at supplied note onsets and does not test that benefit.
T04.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T05.anchorExact: More specifically, the dynamic-level target is formulated as a six-class frame-wise prediction problem, including one \textit{blank} class before the first annotated marking and the five score-dynamics classes used in MazurkaBL: \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}. The change-point target is binary and indicates whether a contextual transition between adjacent dynamic regimes occurs at a given time. Beats and downbeats are also binary frame-wise targets. At inference time, the frame-wise outputs are converted into beat-synchronous score annotations by sampling the dynamic class at beat locations and snapping detected change points to the nearest beat.
T05.proposedEnglish: Changes in the predicted level sequence could also define boundaries. The separate change-point head instead learns an explicit boundary target, while the level head predicts the dynamic state.
T05.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T06.anchorExact: This chapter takes a different and simpler route. Instead of training on synthesised audio with synthetic labels, the front-end estimator is trained directly against real performance audio. The synthesiser is involved at training time only as a differentiable interface that connects predicted velocities to a measurable property of the real recording. This avoids the synthesis-to-performance domain gap that dominates synthetic-data transfer pipelines, at the cost of needing a differentiable supervision interface that is reliable across the instruments of interest.
T06.proposedEnglish: This chapter instead adapts a piano-pretrained estimator using real performance audio, without requiring target-domain velocity labels. A differentiable renderer or proxy supplies the training signal. Its match to the target recordings remains a limitation.
T06.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T07.anchorExact: The advantage of this interface is that it exposes the front end to rich waveform gradients. The risk, already noted in Section~\ref{sec:bp:related}, is that any timbral or recording mismatch between $\tilde{a}$ and $a$ also enters the gradient. When the synthesiser is not a faithful match for the target recordings, the gradient can become dominated by nuisance compensation rather than by velocity correction.
T07.proposedEnglish: The waveform interface supplies gradients through a differentiable approximation of the instrument. Its timbre and velocity response may differ from the target recordings. The observed degradation is consistent with this mismatch, but reconstruction fidelity and velocity-gradient accuracy were not measured separately on the target recordings.
T07.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T08.anchorExact: Referring to Figure~\ref{fig:intro_overview}, the core methodological chapters (Chapters 3--5) preserve the technical contributions of their respective peer-reviewed publications, adapted to form a unified narrative.
T08.proposedEnglish: Chapters 3--6 are based on the four co-authored studies listed in the Authorship Declaration. The thesis brings them together through a common label-recovery question, a shared account of dynamics representations, and the cross-chapter discussion of assumptions and limitations in Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}.
T08.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T09.anchorExact: Second, the strongest direct supervision in the thesis remains piano-centric. This reflects the state of available velocity-labelled datasets rather than a belief that piano dynamics is the universal template for all instruments. Chapter~\ref{ch:beyondpiano} addresses this bias by moving into a label-scarce guitar setting, but the broader point remains: once the target instrument lacks direct performance-control labels, the interpretation of recovered velocity must be stated operationally.
T09.proposedEnglish: Second, the strongest direct supervision remains piano-based. Chapter~\ref{ch:beyondpiano} extends the approach to guitar using renderer-conditioned velocity and loudness-based evaluation. Voice, bowed strings, and wind instruments were not evaluated; their sustained and continuous controls would require targets and acoustic descriptors beyond the attack-focused PHE/OSF pair.
T09.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T10.anchorExact:
Although a substantial gap to human performance remains, the proposed U-Net clearly outperforms the other systems.
The Flat model performs worst, consistent with earlier findings that default velocity is musically inadequate \cite{kuo2021velocity}.
The seen, less-seen, and unseen repertoire groups are best interpreted as descriptive groups rather than as a strict complexity-controlled comparison.
Even so, the relatively narrow 95\% confidence intervals across groups suggest that participants rated the stimuli with reasonable consistency.
T10.proposedEnglish: U-Net received higher mean similarity ratings than Flat and ConvAE on the selected excerpts, while Flat received the lowest ratings, consistent with earlier findings on default velocity \cite{kuo2021velocity}. The listening study provides supplementary perceptual evidence from 11 expert listeners, eight selected SMD excerpts, and one PianoTeq rendering configuration. The composer-group scores are descriptive rather than a controlled comparison of stylistic effects.
T10.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

N01.anchorExact: To test dynamics sensitivity, $\Delta(\mathrm{GT} - \mathrm{Flat\,64})$ asks whether a metric can distinguish expressive resynthesis from a flat one. Among the similarity metrics, Pearson $r$ produces the larger separation on both BSSL ($+0.118$) and BSTL ($+0.263$). Cosine similarity also orders GT above flat, but it severely compresses the margin ($+0.052$ on BSSL and $+0.047$ on BSTL), proving \emph{insensitive} to fine dynamics differences.
N01.proposedEnglish: Both similarity metrics score GT above flat velocity in this diagnostic. Their numerical GT--flat gaps do not by themselves establish which metric is more sensitive to dynamics.
N01.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

N02.anchorExact: To evaluate renderer robustness, $\Delta\lvert\mathrm{Sal.} - \mathrm{YDP}\rvert$ asks whether a metric is stable when the rendering SoundFont is swapped while the underlying note velocities are kept the same. Here, MAE proves \emph{over-sensitive} to absolute gain: it drifts by $0.193$ on BSSL and $1.723$ on BSTL, substantially more than the corresponding drift on $r$ ($0.034$ and $0.011$). On real recordings, this drift would conflate dynamics differences with renderer choice and make the evaluation unreliable.
N02.proposedEnglish: Changing from Salamander to YDP retains the GT notes and velocities but changes their rendered sound. This comparison tests the renderer change as a whole, rather than gain alone.
N02.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

T11.anchorExact: The Huber form tolerates outliers from onset contamination such as overlapping notes, while the parameter-space objective concentrates gradients on note intensity and attack behaviour rather than on waveform details that are weakly related to velocity.
T11.proposedEnglish: We chose Huber for its smooth gradients near zero and L1-like penalty for large residuals. We have not established an advantage over MAE.
T11.candidateVersion: final reviewed v5 proposal; not author approved

V4-velocity-1.anchorExact: Originating from the physical sensors of electronic keyboards and pianos, MIDI velocity is a machine-centric measurement of physical intensity. To say it operates as a "note-level" parameter means that every music note from a discrete key strike is assigned an independent, static integer representing its initial strike force. This strict per-note measurement dictates that velocity functions as a discrete loudness control parameter. It is highly granular and absolute within its own scale, yet the resulting loudness highly depends on the acoustic environment and the specific instrument being played. Because MIDI velocity is necessary for MIDI-to-audio playback in DAWs and synthesisers, a common default is set to 64 when it is missing.
V4-velocity-1.proposedEnglish: Here, MIDI velocity refers to the velocity value in a Note On message. It is a machine-readable control parameter. In sensor-equipped piano data, the recorded value acts as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion. Each note carries an integer value that can be edited independently, although its acoustic effect depends on the instrument and renderer. When expressive values are missing, a MIDI sequence may instead use a constant such as 64.

V4-R1-33-common-3.anchorExact: Velocity is not the only MIDI control that shapes rendered dynamics: continuous controllers can also encode within-note loudness variation~\cite{ryu2024midfild}. Pedal settings and room response also affect the synthesised piano waveform and are explicitly modelled by DDSP-Piano~\cite{renault2023ddsp_piano}. Consequently, when adaptation updates only velocity, the velocity gradient can become entangled with residuals caused by fixed or unobserved controls. Diff-SFProxy avoids this contamination by treating velocity as the only loudness-shaping degree of freedom, but the choice carries its own cost. The recovered velocity absorbs effects that, in the real performance, came from other parallel controls.
V4-R1-33-common-3.proposedEnglish: Velocity is not the only MIDI control that shapes rendered dynamics: continuous controllers can also encode within-note loudness variation~\cite{ryu2024midfild}. Pedal settings and room response also affect the synthesised piano waveform and are explicitly modelled by DDSP-Piano~\cite{renault2023ddsp_piano}. Consequently, when adaptation updates only velocity, the velocity gradient can become entangled with residuals caused by fixed or unobserved controls. Diff-SFProxy restricts the adapted control to velocity, but this does not remove effects of unobserved controls from the target audio. The recovered velocity may therefore absorb effects that, in the real performance, came from other parallel controls.

R1-09-note-on-definition.anchorExact: MIDI velocity is a different kind of representation. It is attached to a note onset rather than to a phrase or region. In conventional MIDI performance data, a sounding note onset carries a discrete velocity value on a finite integer scale. In a chord, each note may have a different velocity. MIDI velocity is therefore a micro-level representation: it serialises note-level actions rather than summarising the expressive state of a passage.

sectionPath.section_title: MIDI velocity as micro-level performance control

R1-09-note-on-definition.contextAfter: The word \emph{velocity} is often described informally as key-strike force. For keyboard instruments this is useful but imprecise. In sensor-equipped acoustic pianos, the recorde

R1-09-existing-calibration-KEEP.anchorExact:
The word \emph{velocity} is often described informally as key-strike force. For keyboard instruments this is useful but imprecise. In sensor-equipped acoustic pianos, the recorded value is more accurately treated as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion near the note attack. Studies of computer-controlled pianos distinguish the player's physical action, the hammer--string interaction, the measured control value, and the resulting acoustic signal \cite{goebl2003role,goebl2004piano}. Large piano datasets such as MAESTRO use this property to provide aligned audio and MIDI data with key-strike velocity labels, making note-level velocity a practical target for MIR systems \cite{hawthorne2019maestro}.

MIDI velocity is exact as symbolic data. A note with velocity 80 remains velocity 80 when the MIDI file is copied, edited, or passed to a model. It is also mechanical in the sense that it refers to a local performance control: how strongly a note attack is executed or how strongly a synthesiser should respond. This objectivity is one reason why velocity is attractive for automatic transcription, expressive rendering, and symbolic performance modelling \cite{ewert2011est,kim2023score,kim2024method}.

However, exactness in the data structure does not imply universality in sound. MIDI velocity is not loudness, not amplitude, and not a dynamic marking. It is a control parameter whose acoustic effect depends on the instrument, renderer, register, sample layer, synthesis design, and recording chain. Dannenberg's analysis of MIDI velocity shows that different synthesisers and patches implement substantially different velocity-response curves \cite{dan2006psy}. Thus, a MIDI value can be objective without being perceptually absolute. It is exact as a note-level control value, but relative as an acoustic and musical quantity.

They include static markings such as \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mp}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}, as well as directional indications such as \textit{crescendo}, \textit{diminuendo}, and hairpins. R1-12-scope-crossref.anchorExact: From a machine-learning perspective, score-dynamics recovery can be framed as classification or structured sequence labelling. The input is audio. The output is a sequence of dynamic symbols or dynamic regimes. The choice of audio representation is therefore not neutral. In the MazurkaBL line of work, the performed-loudness side of this mapping is extracted through sone-based psychoacoustic processing rather than raw amplitude, precisely because the target concerns perceived intensity rather than unweighted energy \cite{kosta2017thesis}. More generally, perceptual front-ends such as Bark-scale specific loudness preserve both a scalar loudness trajectory and the Bark-wise distribution of loudness across the spectrum, which gives a better inductive bias for loudness-oriented tasks than log-Mel features \cite{narang2024automatic,he2026dynest}. Figure~\ref{fig:bg_temporal_units}(a)--(c) shows this contrast on the same excerpt. The practical consequence is also clear: a Nyquist-constrained Bark front-end is substantially lower-dimensional than a $128$-band log-Mel representation, which enables longer audio segments and the phrase-level context that score dynamics actually requires. The challenge is that the labels themselves are sparse, relative, and musically contextual rather than physically absolute. This is one reason why a beat-synchronous formulation is more natural than direct frame-wise regression of continuous loudness.

R1-14-definitions.anchorExact: Score dynamics is usually evaluated as classification on a musically meaningful grid. F1 score is common because the class distribution is imbalanced and because some symbols occur much less frequently than others \cite{kosta2017thesis}. In the present thesis, beat-synchronous evaluation is especially important because it avoids arbitrary frame-level tolerance choices and aligns the prediction target with how the annotations are actually used in music notation.
R1-14-definitions.proposedEnglish: For a given class or event type, precision is TP/(TP+FP), recall is TP/(TP+FN), and F1 is 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN), where TP, FP, and FN are true positives, false positives, and false negatives. Macro-F1 averages the class-wise scores equally, whereas support-weighted F1 weights them by their reference counts. These averages answer different questions and must be identified when reporting score-dynamics results. Note-level velocity MAE averages the absolute prediction error over the reference note onsets; its full definition and the complementary dispersion metrics are given in Section 3.6.3.

R1-17-OFV-KEEP.anchorExact:
To process MIDI as images, we convert each performance into three matrices of size \(T \times P\), where \(T\) is the number of time frames and \(P=88\) is the number of piano pitches.
The three matrices are a binary onset roll \(O\), marking note starts; a binary frame roll \(F\), indicating note activation over time; and a velocity roll \(V\), acting as the target colour intensity.
In the implemented system, \(F\) is the network input, \(V\) is the prediction target, and \(O\) is used for onset masking in the loss.
For the velocity roll, integer values in \([0,127]\) are normalised to \([0,1)\) to match the model output activation range.
During post-processing, the model output is denormalised by scaling and rounding back to integer MIDI velocity.
As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:velcomp_model}, these matrices are highly sparse.

R1-19-existing-task-KEEP.anchorExact: MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) is the dominant symbolic format in modern music production. A MIDI file that resembles sheet music can still sound mechanical when its note velocities are undefined or flattened to a default constant. In contrast, MIDI captured from human performance preserves the performer's control of intensity and therefore carries a substantial portion of the perceived musical expression. As discussed in the thesis introduction, dynamics is the expressive dimension targeted first in this thesis because it is both perceptually salient and directly editable. This chapter studies the most constrained setting in that map: recovering note-level MIDI velocity when the symbolic notes and their timing are already known.

R1-21-procedure-reference-KEEP.anchorExact:
\paragraph{Procedure.}
Participants were instructed to use headphones because the relevant velocity differences are subtle and are easier to judge at adequate playback quality and level.
In each trial, the audio rendered from the human-performed MIDI served as the fixed reference, and the rendered system outputs were judged relative to that reference.
Following a MUSHRA-inspired reference-based procedure \cite{series2014mursha}, participants rated each processed stimulus independently on a continuous 0--5 scale, where the labelled intervals corresponded to ``bad'', ``poor'', ``fair'', ``good'', and ``excellent'' similarity.
The final scores were averaged across listeners to obtain MOS, and 95\% confidence intervals were computed for reporting.

R1-27-complete-amt-boundary.anchorExact: Given a piano performance audio signal, the system predicts four synchronised output sequences on a frame grid: dynamic levels, dynamic change points, beats, and downbeats. The dynamic targets are the score-facing outputs, while beats and downbeats provide the metrical structure required to align these labels to a symbolic score. This joint design serves two practical modes of use. In the first mode, a reliable beat grid is already available from an aligned score or a score-level AMT system, and the predicted dynamic labels are attached to that grid. In the second mode, no score is available, and the model first predicts beats and downbeats by itself, then uses the estimated grid to place the dynamic labels.

R1-30-label-prior-discussion-evidence.anchorExact: The cross-dataset results make this distinction more concrete. If score dynamics were merely a continuous loudness variable relabelled into five fixed bins, an out-of-domain corpus with compatible audio quality would mainly cause smooth calibration errors. Instead, Vienna4x22 shows that the symbolic prior itself matters: a passage that is moderate in acoustic intensity may be notated as \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, or \textit{f} depending on the local phrase, edition, and corpus convention. A model trained on MazurkaBL carries a learned expectation about how often each of these labels should occur, and this expectation can become wrong even when the metrical grid remains reasonably stable. The model is therefore learning an acoustic, metrical, and editorial mapping at the same time.
